summary: Defines a format for bibliographic records that describe technical reports. It is intended for exchanging catalogue-style information about reports, and is an informational document.

eli5.summary: A standard library index card for describing research reports, so different libraries can swap them.

subtitle: A plain-text, tag-based record format for describing technical reports so libraries can swap catalogue entries by email or file transfer.

tldr.problem: Universities announced new technical reports by mailing paper records, which cost money, took time and could not be filed or searched electronically.
tldr.mechanism: A simple record of tagged fields, each written as a tag, two colons and its data, that people can read and write in any text editor, with a few mandatory fields and many optional ones.
tldr.outcome: An Informational format used by the Cornell Dienst protocol and the Stanford SIFT system; it revises and obsoletes RFC 1357 with new fields such as handle, other_access, keyword and withdraw.

today: RFC 1807 is an Informational memo from June 1995 that obsoletes RFC 1357. According to the metadata for this page, no later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a Common Record Format
sections.content:
Many universities and R&D organizations announce new technical reports by posting the bibliographic records on paper. That has real cost and delay, and recipients cannot conveniently file the records electronically for later searches. This RFC offers a format that can be sent by e-mail or file transfer instead.

The format is a tagged one with self-explaining alphabetic tags, made to be easy for both people and programs. It defines the format of the records, not how to process them. The RFC says the format was used by the Dienst system and by five ARPA-funded computer science institutions, and that programs had been written to map between it and USMARC cataloging records.
sections.eli5: Instead of mailing paper cards about new research reports, schools can send the same information as plain text that anyone can open.

sections.title: The Meta Format
sections.content:
A record describes one publication and contains several fields. Each field starts with a tag at the beginning of a line (spaces before it are allowed), followed by two colons, ::, and then the field data. Tags are reserved identifiers with no separators in them.

Lines are limited to 79 characters. A field can continue over several lines with an implied space between them, and there is no special continuation marker. A field simply ends where the next line starts with a word followed by two colons. Indenting continuation lines is suggested for readability.

Only printable ASCII characters (codes 040 through 176) and line breaks are allowed. Tabs must be replaced by spaces, and tabs, nulls, DEL and backspaces make a record invalid. Full 8-bit ASCII may be used, but some mailers cannot handle it.
sections.eli5: Every line starts with a label and two colons, then the information. If the information is long, it just keeps going on the next lines.

sections.title: Mandatory Fields and Record Identity
sections.content:
Four fields are mandatory, and a record without them is invalid: BIB-VERSION, ID, ENTRY and END. They must be the first, second, third and last fields, and may not be repeated. All other fields may appear in any order and may be repeated, and the order of repeated fields is preserved.

BIB-VERSION names the format version, which for this RFC is CS-TR-v2.1. Versions starting with X are experimental and should NOT be put in the recipient's permanent database. ID has the form publisher-ID//free-text, for example OUKS//CS-TR-91-123, and the publisher symbols DUMMY and TEST mark test records. ENTRY is the date the record was created, in the form January 15, 1992. END repeats the same ID that began the record.

The RFC suggests that publishers register their symbols and names, and says Rebecca Lasher agreed to coordinate this with the IANA for computer science technical report publishers.
sections.eli5: Every card needs four things: what version of the form it is, a unique number, the date it was made, and an ending line that repeats the number.

sections.title: Optional Descriptive Fields
sections.content:
Everything else is optional. TITLE, AUTHOR (personal names, last name first), CORP-AUTHOR, CONTACT, DATE, PAGES, ORGANIZATION (full name, no acronyms), TYPE and SERIES describe the report. FUNDING, MONITORING, CONTRACT and GRANT record who paid for and oversaw the work, and LANGUAGE defaults to English if omitted.

Access fields include HANDLE, which MUST be supplied if the report is available in electronic form and has the form hdl:naming authority/string. OTHER_ACCESS holds one URL or URN per occurrence and RETRIEVAL is free text on how to get the full text. KEYWORD, CR-CATEGORY (a Computer Reviews category such as D.0), NOTES and ABSTRACT help searching. The abstract is highly recommended, preferably in English, and applications should not be expected to handle more than 10,000 characters of it.
sections.eli5: The rest of the card is extras: who wrote it, how long it is, where to find it, a few search words, and a short summary.

sections.title: Revisions and Withdrawals
sections.content:
A REVISION field marks a record as replacing an earlier one. It has a date, optionally followed by a semicolon and free text describing the change, and any record with a more recent revision date completely replaces an earlier one. A revised record is complete, not a list of changes. A revision date of 0 is read as January 1, 1900, to support records from RFC 1357.

A WITHDRAW field says the document is no longer available, with the reason in free text. A withdraw record carries all mandatory fields, the WITHDRAW field and a mandatory REVISION field. Each institution decides whether to delete withdrawn records or only some of their fields.

The RFC does not limit who may receive the records. If the publication itself should be restricted, it should be protected by some other means such as passwords, which the RFC does not address.
sections.eli5: If a card has a mistake, you send a new full card with a newer date. If a report is taken away, you send a card saying it was withdrawn and why.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 1357
sections.content:
This RFC is a revision of RFC 1357, written by D. Cohen in July 1992. The abstract lists the new fields: HANDLE, OTHER_ACCESS, KEYWORD and WITHDRAW. The BIB-VERSION is now CS-TR-v2.1.

The RFC includes the CR-CATEGORY field for computer science and says similar fields are expected for other domains. Its security section states that security issues are not discussed.
sections.eli5: This is the second version of the card. It added boxes for a permanent ID, web links, keywords and a note that a report was withdrawn.

data.title: Withdrawing a record
data.code:
BIB-VERSION::  CS-TR-v2.1
ID::           OUKS//CS-TR-91-123
ENTRY::        January 21, 1995
ORGANIZATION:: Oceanview University, Kansas, Computer
               Science
TITLE::        The Computerization of Oceanview with
               High Speed Fiber Optics Communication
REVISION::     January 21, 1995
WITHDRAW::     Withdrawn, found to be irrelevant
END::          OUKS//CS-TR-91-123
